A) Digital humans are coming to a screen near you. As computer-generated imagery (CGI) has become cheaper and more sophisticated, the film industry can now convincingly recreate people on screen— even actors who have been dead for decades. The technology's ability to effectively keep celebrities alive beyond the grave is raising questions about public legacies and image rights.
B) Late in 2019, it was announced that US actor James Dean, who died in 1955, will star in a Vietnam War film scheduled for release later this year. In the film, which will be called Finding Jack, Dean will be recreated on screen with CGI based on old footage(影片镜头) and photographs, with another actor voicing him. The news was met with excitement by those keen to see Dean digitally brought back to life for only his fourth film, but it also drew sharp criticism. "This is puppeteering the dead for their fame alone," actress Zelda Williams wrote on Twitter. "It sets such an awful precedent for the future of performance." Her father, Robin Williams, who died in 2014, was keen to avoid the same fate. Before his death, he filed a deed protecting the use of his image until 2039, preventing others from recreating him using CGI to appear in a film, TV show or as a hologram(全息影像).
C) The James Dean film is a way to keep the actor's image relevant for younger generations, says Mark Roesler of CMG Worldwide, the firm that represents Dean's estate. "I think this is the beginning of an entire wave," says Travis Cloyd, CEO of Worldwide XR, one of the companies behind the digital recreation of Dean. "Moving into the future, we want James Dean to be brought into different gaming environments, or different virtual reality environments, or augmented reality environments," he says.
D) Other actors have been revived, with the permission of their estates, for advertising purposes: for example, a 2011 advertisement for Dior featured contemporary actress Charlize Theron alongside iconic 20th-century stars Marilyn Monroe, Grace Kelly and Marlene Dietrich. Later, Audrey Hepburn was digitally recreated for a chocolate commercial in 2013. In the same year, a CGI Bruce Lee appeared in a Chinese-language ad for a whisky brand, which offended many fans because Lee was widely known not to drink alcohol at all. "In the last five years, it's become more affordable and more achievable in a whole movie," says Tim Webber at UK visual effects firm Framestore, the company behind the Hepburn chocolate ad. Framestore used body doubles with resemblance to Hepburn's facial structure and body shape as a framework for manual animation. The process was extremely difficult and expensive, says Webber, but the technology has moved on.
E) Now, a person can be animated from scratch. "If they're alive today, you can put them in scanning rigs, you can get every detail of their body analysed very carefully and that makes it much easier, whereas working from available photographs is tricky," says Webber, who won an Academy Award for his visual effects work on the 2013 film Gravity. "I also see a lot of actors today who will have the desire to take advantage of this technology: to have their likeness captured and stored for future content," says Cloyd. "They foresee this being something that could give their estates and give their families the ability to make money from their likeness when they're gone."
F) A hidden hazard of digitally recreating a deceased(已故的) celebrity is the risk of damaging their legacy. "We have to respect the security and the integrity of rights holders," says John Canning at Digital Domain, a US firm that created a hologram rapper(说唱艺人) Tupac Shakur, which appeared at the Coachella music festival in 2012, 15 years after his death.
G) Legally, a person's rights to control the commercial use of their name and image beyond their death differ between and even within countries. In certain US states, for example, these rights are treated similarly to property rights, and are transferable to a person's heirs. In California, under the Celebrities Rights Act, the personality rights for a celebrity last for 70 years after their death. "We've got a societal debate going on about access to our public commons, as it were, about famous faces," says Lilian Edwards at Newcastle University, UK. Should the public be allowed to use or reproduce images of famous people, given how iconic they are? And what is in the best interest of a deceased person's legacy may conflict with the desires of their family or the public, says Edwards.
H) A recreation, however lifelike, will never be indistinguishable from a real actor, says Webber. "When we are bringing someone back, representing someone who is no longer alive on the screen, what we are doing is extremely sophisticated digital make-up," he says: "A performance is a lot more than a physical resemblance."
I) As it becomes easier to digitally recreate celebrities and to entirely manufacture on-screen identities, could this kind of technology put actors out of jobs? "I think actors are worried about this," says Edwards. "But I think it will take a very long time." This is partly because of the risk that viewers find virtual humans scary. Edwards cites widespread backlash to the digital recreation of Carrie Fisher as a young Princess Leia in Rogue One, a trick later repeated in the recent Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker, which was filmed after Fisher's death in 2016. "People didn't like it," she says. "They discovered the uncanny valley(诡异谷)."
J) This refers to the idea that when objects trying to resemble humans aren't quite perfect, they can make viewers feel uneasy because they fall somewhere between obviously non-human and fully human. "That's always a danger when you're doing anything human or human-like," says Webber. "There're a thousand things that could go wrong with a computer-generated facial performance, and any one of those could make it fall into the uncanny valley," he says: "Your brain just knows there's something wrong." The problem often arises around the eyes or mouth, says Webber. "They're the areas that you look at when you're talking to someone."
K) An unfamiliar digital human that has been created through CGI will also face the same challenge as an unknown actor: they don't have the appeal of an established name. "You have to spend substantial capital in creating awareness around their likeness and making sure people are familiar with who they are," says Cloyd. This is now starting to happen. "The way you pre-sell a movie in a foreign market is based on relevant talent," he says. "I think we're a long way away from having virtual beings that have the ability to pre-sell content."
L) Webber expects that we will see more digital humans on screen. "It's happening because it can happen," he says. Referring to a line from Jurassic Park(侏罗纪公园), he adds: "People are too busy thinking about what they can do to think about whether they should do it." 36. There is an ongoing debate among the public as to whether the images of deceased celebrities should be recreated.

P1 You can't see it, smell it, or hear it, and people disagree on how precisely to define it, or where exactly it comes from. It isn't a school subject or an academic discipline, but it can be learned. It is a quality that is required of artists, but it is also present in the lives of scientists and entrepreneurs. All of us benefit from it and we thrive mentally and spiritually when we are able to wield it. It is a delicate thing, easily stamped out; in fact, it flourishes most fully when people are playful and childlike. Meanwhile, it works best in conjunction with deep knowledge and expertise.

P2 This mysterious—but teachable—quality is creativity, the subject of a recently-published report by Durham Commission on Creativity and Education. The report concludes that creativity should not inhabit the school curriculum only as it relates to drama, music, art and other obviously creative subjects, but that creative thinking ought to run through all of school life, infusing(充满) the way humanities and natural sciences are learned. Questions 46 to 50 are based on the following passage.

P3 The authors, who focus on education in England, offer a number of sensible recommendations, some of which are an attempt to alleviate the uninspiring and fact-based approach to education that has crept into policy in recent years. When children are regarded as vessels to be filled with facts, creativity does not prosper; nor does it when teachers' sole objective is coaching children towards exams. One suggestion from the commission is a network of teacher-led "creativity collaboratives", along the lines of existing maths hubs( 中心), with the aim of supporting teaching for creativity through the school curriculum.

P4 Nevertheless, it is arts subjects through which creativity can most obviously be fostered. The value placed on them by the independent education sector is clear. One only has to look at the remarkable arts facilities at Britain's top private schools to comprehend this. But in the state sector the excessive focus on English, maths and science threatens to crush arts subjects; meanwhile, reduced school budgets mean diminishing extracurricular activities. There has been a 28.1% decline in students taking creative subjects at high schools since 2014, though happily, art and design have seen a recent increase.

P5 This discrepancy between state and private education is a matter of social justice. It is simply wrong and unfair that most children have a fraction of the access to choirs, orchestras, art studios and drama that their more privileged peers enjoy. As lives are affected by any number of looming challenges —climate crisis, automation in the workplace—humans are going to need creative thinking more than ever. For all of our sakes, creativity in education, and for all, must become a priority.

P1 Emulating your conversation partner's actions is a common human behavior classified as "mirroring" and has been known and studied by psychologists for years. We all tend to subconsciously copy gestures of people we like. But why do we act like this?

P2 As a rule, mirroring means that conversationalists enjoy their communication and that there's a certain level of agreement between them. The topic of discussion is equally interesting for both and they know their interests meet.

P3 Repeating someone's behavior is typical of talented communicators, not always because the person is sympathetic, but because there is a goal to be achieved. This way new idols have been brought to the stage: politicians, celebrities, and other big names. Popular culture makes people want to look popular, and act and speak like popular people. Questions 51 to 55 are based on the following passage.

P4 Nowadays celebrities steal lyrics from each other and struggle with copyright violation accusations or straightforwardly claim themselves to be the authors, even though all the work was done by other people.

P5 Among celebrities, it's trendy nowadays to use their own speech writers as politicians do. The so-called "ghostwriting" can take various forms: books, articles, autobiographies, and even social media posts.

P6 Who is a true copycat(抄袭者) and who gets copycatted? Sometimes, it is a hard nut to crack without an expert's help. But new authorship defending methods based on identifying individual writing patterns are already here. Their aim is to protect intellectual property. Using scientific methods, some of them can define authorship with 85% accuracy.

P7 Writing is not an easy craft to master. If you want to write like a professional without plagiarism(抄袭), there are a few lessons to learn and the first one is: "Copy from one, it's plagiarism; copy from two, it's research." The correct interpretation of this statement is not about copying, but rather about creating your own style. When you study an author's writing style, don't stop on a single one, but explore numerous styles instead. Examine types of sentences they use, pay attention to their metaphors, and focus on stories you feel you could write a pretty cool sequel(续篇) to.

P8 Imitation is rather paradoxical. As an integral part of learning, it brings about positive changes, making people develop and grow. However, it may do a lot of harm. Copying someone's thoughts, ideas or inventions is completely unacceptable. It infringes on intellectual property rights of others.

P9 Still, many things we do are about copying others one way or another. So if you want to compliment someone on the work they have done and imitate it, just make sure you do it the right way to avoid committing plagiarism.

writing.directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write an essay based on the chart below. You should start your essay with a brief description of the chart and comment on China's achievements in poverty alleviation. You should write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.model: The chart clearly illustrates the striking decline of rural poverty in China from 2012 to 2020. During this period, the rural poor population plunged from around 98 million to nearly zero, while the incidence of poverty fell in parallel from about 10.2% to almost 0%. Based on official statistics, this downward trend remained remarkably steady throughout the whole period. Several factors account for this remarkable achievement. Above all, the Chinese government made poverty alleviation a national priority and rolled out a series of targeted measures, such as developing local industries, relocating residents from harsh areas and improving education. These well-designed policies steadily lifted millions of people out of poverty. The significance of this progress can hardly be overstated. Not only has it dramatically improved the livelihood of the rural population, but it also offers a valuable model for other developing nations still fighting poverty. In my view, such an accomplishment fully demonstrates what determination and effective governance can bring about.

成因主句加实例回扣。本段落实了'成因分点加实例'：'Several factors account for this remarkable achievement' 作过渡兼主句，'such as developing local industries, relocating residents... and improving education' 用实例撑起成因，末句 'These well-designed policies steadily lifted millions of people out of poverty' 把举措与结果回扣，评论有据不空喊。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干 Yunnan is a province（主语策略：原句主语） 中文已有明确主语"云南"，直接作英文主语；核心是判断关系 云南是位于中国西南的一个省份，谓 语用 is、表语用 a province，立起 Yunnan is a province 这一骨架。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 两个修饰各自降级 主干外有两块："位于中国西南的"修饰 province，降级成介词短语 in southwest China 作后置定 语（province in southwest China）；"平均海拔1500米"是另一项数据，降级成介词短语 with an average altitude of 1,500 meters 挂在后面，避免另起一句和中文一样平铺。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 时态 回指全篇基调，用一般现在时 is——这是云南长期为真的属性，非过去事件。 冠词 "一个省份"是泛指其中之一，用不定冠词 a province；不要漏冠词写成 is province。 数字与单位 "1500米"写成 1,500 meters，meter 可数且数量大于一，用复数 meters；altitude/elevation 表 海拔均可。

sentences.label: 译文
sentences.text: Yunnan is a province in southwest China, with an average altitude of 1,500 meters. 2. 云南历史悠久，风景秀丽，气候宜人。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干 It has / It boasts（主语策略：原句主语） 三个四字短语 云南历史悠久，风景秀丽，气候宜人 实为"云南拥有 X、Y、Z"，主语仍是云南（用 It 承接上句），核心动词补一个"拥有"义的 has 或 boasts，把三项并列宾语统起来：It has a long history, beautiful scenery and a pleasant climate。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 三短语并列作宾语 "历史悠久→a long history""风景秀丽→beautiful scenery""气候宜人→a pleasant climate"三项 是同级并列，用 A, B and C 结构挂在 has/boasts 后；不必拆成三句，更不要用三个 and 串成流 水句。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 时态 回指基调用一般现在时 has/boasts。 单复数与冠词 scenery 是不可数名词，不加 a、不加 s；history 和 climate 在此为可数的具体一项，配 a long history、a pleasant climate。 搭配 "气候宜人"地道搭配是 a pleasant/mild climate；"风景秀丽"用 beautiful scenery 或 picturesque scenery。

sentences.label: 译文
sentences.text: It has a long history, beautiful scenery and a pleasant climate. 3. 云南生态环境优越，生物多种多样，被誉为野生动植物的天堂。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干落在"被誉为"（主语策略：原句主语） 本句三小句里，最核心的动作是末句 被誉为野生动植物的天堂——是个被动表达。主语仍是云南 （It），主干定为 It is known/honored as a paradise，前两小句"生态环境优越，生物多种多 样"作为原因降级处理。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 原因降级成with短语 "生态环境优越，生物多种多样"是云南被誉为天堂的原因，降级成 With its superior ecological environment and diverse species 这个 with 引导的伴随/原因状语，置于句首；主句保留 it is known as a paradise for wild animals and plants，避免照中文排成三个并列小句。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 语态 "被誉为"是被动，用 is known as / is honored as / is reputed as；英文被动远多于汉语，此处必 须保留被动。 单复数 "野生动植物"含多种，animals and plants 用复数；"生物多种多样"译 diverse species，species 单复数同形、此处表复数概念。 搭配 "天堂"用 a paradise，后接 for：a paradise for wild animals and plants；"生态环 境"ecological environment。

sentences.label: 译文
sentences.text: With its superior ecological environment and diverse species, it is known as a paradise for wild animals and plants. 4. 云南还有多种矿藏和充足的水资源,为全省经济的可持续发展提供了有利条件。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干 It also has resources（主语策略：原句主语） 主语仍是云南（It），核心动词是"有"，宾语是 多种矿藏和充足的水资源，立骨架 It also has various mineral resources and abundant water resources；后半"为…提供了有利条件"是 这"有"带来的结果，降级处理。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 结果用现在分词承接 "为全省经济的可持续发展提供了有利条件"降级成现在分词短语 providing favorable conditions for the sustainable development of the province's economy，作结果状语挂在主句后；与主句 共用主语 It，无需重复主语、也不用 and 另起一句。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 时态 中文"提供了"的"了"易诱人用过去时，但这是云南资源"一直在"提供的条件、属持续事实，回指基 调仍用一般现在时（分词 providing 不带时态、随主句现在时）。 单复数 "多种矿藏"various mineral resources 用复数；resource 表"资源"作可数复数 resources，water resources 同。 搭配与冠词 "可持续发展"sustainable development（不可数，不加 a）；"有利条件"favorable conditions；"充足的"abundant/sufficient。

sentences.label: 译文
sentences.text: It also has various mineral resources and abundant water resources, providing favorable conditions for the sustainable development of the province's economy. 5. 云南居住着25个少数民族,他们大多有自己的语言、习俗和宗教。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干 It is home to / 25 minorities live（主语策略：原句主语） 前半 云南居住着25个少数民族 主干可处理成 It is home to 25 ethnic minorities（地道地表"是… 的聚居地"），主语云南→It；后半"他们大多有…"另立主干 most of whom have…，用关系代词 whom 把后半挂成定语从句。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 后半改非限定定语从句 "他们大多有自己的语言、习俗和宗教"中的"他们"指代前面的 25 个少数民族，改用 most of whom have their own languages, customs and religions 接成非限定定语从句，避免另起一句 重复 they 作主语；三项并列宾语用 A, B and C。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 单复数 "25个少数民族"复数 25 ethnic minorities；"语言、习俗和宗教"对应每个民族各有，用复数 languages, customs and religions。 主谓一致 定语从句 most of whom 指代复数的 minorities，谓语用复数 have，不是 has。 代词搭配 "自己的"用 their own，与复数先行词一致；their own 强调"各自拥有"。

sentences.label: 译文
sentences.text: It is home to 25 ethnic minorities, most of whom have their own languages, customs and religions. 6. 云南独特的自然景色和丰富的民族文化使其成为中国最受欢迎的旅游目的地之一，每年都吸 引着大批国内外游客前往观光旅游。

sentences.label: 主干
sentences.text: 主干 Scenery and culture make it…（主语策略：原句主语） 本句核心是"使…成为"的使役结构 使其成为中国最受欢迎的旅游目的地之一：主语是"独特的自然景 色和丰富的民族文化"，谓语 make，宾语 it（云南），宾补 one of the most popular tourist destinations in China，立起 make sb./sth. + 宾补 的骨架。

sentences.label: 降级
sentences.text: 后半改现在分词状语 "每年都吸引着大批国内外游客前往观光旅游"与前半同主语（自然景色和民族文化），降级成现在 分词短语 attracting large numbers of tourists from home and abroad every year，作伴随状 语挂在主句后；"前往观光旅游"含义已并入 attracting…tourists，无需逐字另译 to visit。

sentences.label: 语法
sentences.text: 主谓一致 主语是 scenery and culture 两项并列，视作复数，使役动词用 make（不加 s），不是 makes。 单复数与固定搭配 "…之一"固定结构 one of the + 最高级 + 复数名词：one of the most popular tourist destinations；"大批游客"large numbers of tourists 复数。 习语搭配 "国内外"地道说法 at home and abroad / from home and abroad；不要逐字译成 inside and outside the country。
